title:
Structural Insights
into Erm-Mediated rRNA Methylation
Underlying Antibiotic Resistance
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>SAM-dependent Erm enzymes confer resistance to clinically important MLSB antibiotics (macrolides–lincosamides–streptogramin B) by methylation of the rRNA (rRNA) target. However, the molecular basis of the Erm–rRNA interaction remains poorly understood, hindering the development of effective Erm inhibitors to preserve antibiotic efficacy. Here, we integrate NMR and computational data to investigate the interaction between ErmB, prevalent in pathogenic Gram-positive bacteria, and a minimal RNA substrate mimicking the rRNA target. We demonstrate that Erm–RNA complex formation is critically dependent on the SAM cofactor, which shapes the conformational space of the entire catalytic domain, priming ErmB for specific recognition of its RNA substrate. Using NMR-guided docking, we derive experimentally validated structural models of the ErmB–RNA complex that reveal a vast and dynamic binding interface comprising ErmB’s N- and C-terminal domains, as well as the cationic interdomain cleft. These insights into the Erm enzyme function provide a foundation for the rational design of potent and selective drugs to combat pathogenic bacteria.</jats:p>

title:
Charge-Transfer Dynamics
in Ternary Organic Photovoltaic
Materials Containing Nonfullerene Acceptors: Role of Reaction Temperature
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ternary organic photovoltaic devices incorporating A-D-A type nonfullerene acceptors offer promising enhancements in power conversion efficiency. However, fabrication conditions can introduce impurities that disrupt molecular packing and the charge-transfer (CT) dynamics, thereby reducing performance and stability. This study investigates ultrafast CT dynamics in ternary organic photovoltaics prepared at room temperature (25 °C, ″cold″) and elevated temperature (65 °C, ″hot″) using two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy in combination with computational spectral analysis to elucidate the underlying photophysical processes. While the cold ternary blend preserves chemical purity, enabling efficient CT, the hot blend exhibits a higher level of impurities, resulting in population trapping in intramolecular CT-type/dark states. This impurity-induced trapping promotes nonradiative recombination and suppresses electron transfer pathways. These findings underscore the critical role of controlled fabrication in mitigating energy losses and optimizing ternary organic photovoltaic performance and reliability.</jats:p>

title:
Supramolecular Hexaphyrin
Cage: Cooperative Guest
Binding and Reversible Aromaticity Switching by Proton-Coupled Electron
Transfer
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Coordination-driven self-assembly of a rigidified, antiaromatic β,β’-linked hexaphyrin ligand (1) bearing three meso-pyridyl donors with a trans-platinum(II) diacceptor corner (2) affords a discrete trigonal-prismatic metal–organic cage, CHP, in which two cofacial hexaphyrin decks are held rigidly apart by three Pt(II)-based coordination bridges. Multinuclear NMR spectroscopy, high-resolution ESI-MS, and DOSY establish the assembly as a single, highly symmetric [2 + 3] species, with a solution-state hydrodynamic radius consistent with the DFT-optimized geometry. Electrochemical and spectroelectrochemical studies reveal that CHP undergoes a reversible proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process, interconverting between a 24π-antiaromatic and a 26π-aromatic Hückel state upon combined treatment with a proton source and a mild chemical or electrochemical reductant, demonstrating that the switching behavior of the parent hexaphyrin is preserved within the confined 3D architecture. Furthermore, the electron-poor internal cavity of CHP encapsulates two planar zinc(II) porphyrazine guests in a discrete 1:2 host–guest complex with positive cooperativity, as quantified by UV–vis titration. This work establishes a strategy for embedding the electronic responsiveness of expanded porphyrinoids within discrete, functional supramolecular hosts.</jats:p>

title:
Structural
Evolution Accompanies Selectivity Changes
during the Electrocatalytic Reduction of CO2 on a Vicinal
Cu(310) Pre-Catalyst
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The electrocatalytic reduction reaction of CO2 (CO2RR) on copper remains a key strategy for converting greenhouse gases into valuable chemicals, but its large-scale implementation still requires substantial advances in our fundamental understanding of the selectivity-determining properties. Historically, stepped Cu surfaces were thought to have great potential for selective hydrocarbon production during CO2RR. However, it has recently become clear that this distinct facet dependence does not hold for atomically flat Cu(100) and (111) surfaces with large terraces, which primarily yield hydrogen. The present study addresses how the crystallographic orientation and surface history influence CO2RR performance over Cu(310), a vicinal surface with an intrinsically higher density of step-edge defects. Our results show striking analogies to the nonvicinal surfaces, namely, an initially large H2 selectivity but also the formation during operation of mesoscopic imperfections that play a crucial role in the surface activation and catalytic selectivity toward hydrocarbons. More importantly, we report the deactivation mechanism of our vicinal surface upon extended CO2RR operation, which switches from hydrocarbon formation back to hydrogen. Additionally, we demonstrate how the desired hydrocarbon-product selectivity can be regenerated via in situ electrochemical oxidative treatments. Finally, substantial differences in the deactivation kinetics toward H2 evolution vs CO2RR, depending on the oxidative treatment employed, are unveiled. These findings establish a clear link between surface mesoscale morphology, oxidation dynamics, and catalytic function, highlighting the need for controlled surface/chemical state engineering in CO2RR catalysts. These insights offer practical guidance for designing more stable and efficient copper-based systems for CO2 conversion.</jats:p>

title:
Phosphate-Mediated
Proton Shuttling Governs Nitrate
Electroreduction Selectivity on Copper
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The electrochemical reduction of nitrate (NO3RR) can be carried out at high reaction rates, yet selectivity to desired ammonia/ammonium remains challenging on catalysts like copper due to a soluble nitrite intermediate. We here find the local microenvironment of NO3RR can influence typical catalyst metrics of rate and selectivity to extents on par with those typically attributed to differences in catalyst formulation. Considering a phosphate-buffered pH 7 medium, we find the high NO3RR rates on Cu exceed the buffering capacity, leading to a surface pH ∼ 13. Accounting for the local proton activity to measure reaction rates at fixed overpotential demonstrates rates approximately an order of magnitude greater compared to a bulk pH 13 electrolyte. In the absence of phosphate, nitrite is kinetically more difficult to reduce on Cu than is nitrate. Inclusion of phosphate─regardless of the bulk pH─leads to the onset of nitrite reduction at comparable potentials to nitrate reduction, and ∼2× higher electron selectivity to ammonia/ammonium compared to without phosphate. Grand canonical density functional theory calculations and microkinetic modeling demonstrate that adsorbed phosphate thermodynamically favors proton abstraction from water under reaction conditions, whereas nitrate and nitrite are incapable of doing so. This effectively leads to a surface-mediated pKa of phosphate species that is different than in solution, which changes the local population of hydrogenated phosphates that can participate in proton-transfer events. This adsorbed phosphate─observed by operando surface-enhanced infrared spectroscopy─stabilizes the nitrite intermediate and promotes proton shuttling from water to nitrite, increasing selectivity to ammonia. The presence of a pH gradient further promotes proton shuttling from the bulk electrolyte to exacerbate these trends. Overall, these findings highlight that surface-mediated processes can strongly impact the effective pKa of adsorbed ions relative to those in solution, and can provide additional routes for leveraging the local environment in catalyst design.</jats:p>

title:
Turnovers Drive Supported
Metal Nanoparticle Catalyst
Surface Reconstruction to Kinetically Trapped Metastable Structures
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Supported metal catalysts often operate with high adsorbate coverages that can alter nanoparticle structures as compared to the clean catalyst. Such restructuring is typically described within an equilibrium picture that assumes that nanoparticle structures and adsorbate coverages adopt their thermodynamically preferred state. Here, we challenge this assumption and propose that under conditions of high adsorbate coverage and fast turnovers of surface species, supported metal nanoparticle structures and adsorbate coverages can become kinetically trapped in metastable states. We studied CO adsorption–desorption quasi-equilibrium on Pt/γ-Al2O3 using in situ IR spectroscopy and chemisorption as a function of temperature (300–650 K), CO pressure (10–2–10–4 bar), and visible photon flux (0–2 W cm–2 440 nm photons). The adsorbed CO IR band area increases with temperature and photon flux, contrary to equilibrium predictions of decreasing coverage. Estimates of apparent Pt dispersion and CO desorption rates, along with the reversibility of IR spectral changes, support the hypothesis that when CO turnovers are faster than Pt atomic rearrangements to their equilibrium state, the catalyst is driven into metastable states. We estimate atomic rearrangements time scales of 10–1–10–3 s on CO-covered Pt nanoparticles at ∼500–600 K. Grand-canonical sampling calculations show that equilibrium Pt–CO structures cannot reproduce the experimental IR trends, implying the presence of off-equilibrium coverages, structures, or both. By matching the experimental trend, theory identifies a plausible flat, nonequilibrium free-energy region that can facilitate kinetic trapping of metastable catalyst states. These results highlight the need for theoretical and experimental approaches targeting nonequilibrium structures to establish structure–function relationships in heterogeneous catalysis.</jats:p>

title:
Hypoxia-Driven,
Self-Accelerating Immolative Photosensitizer
Enabling Effective and Safe Photodynamic Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is an emerging cancer treatment modality, but its clinical translation is hindered by the persistent post-PDT phototoxicity of existing photosensitizers. To address this challenge, we herein report a hypoxia-driven, self-accelerating immolative photosensitizer in which PDT itself drives posttherapy detoxification. This is demonstrated with AIE photosensitizers with an N-oxidation-mediated photoinduced electron transfer (PET) feature, which creates a charge-separation state with pronounced electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling feature, enabling efficient intersystem crossing. This N-oxidation thus converts the highly emissive fluorophore TBP into the robust type I photosensitizer TBPO. Critically, the N-O bond could be selectively cleaved by cytochrome P450 reductases under hypoxia, immolating TBPO back to TBP. Unlike previously reported ROS-driven immolative photosensitizers, this hypoxia-mediated immolation does not consume therapeutic ROS and is accelerated by PDT-aggravated hypoxia. Consequently, TBPO exhibits a self-propelled detoxification mechanism, ensuring an initial high PDT efficacy while minimizing residual phototoxicity after therapy. Moreover, this transition process is self-reported by the fluorescence light-up. This molecular design achieves both potent hypoxia-resistant PDT and fail-safe posttreatment safety, addressing two long-standing barriers to clinical PDT. This paradigm shift offers a general design principle for therapy-fueled self-detoxifying photosensitizers toward outpatient PDT without lifestyle restrictions.</jats:p>

title:
Elusive *CH–*CHO
Coupling Pathway for High-Performance
CO2 Electroreduction to n-Propanol
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to high-value n-propanol represents a promising yet challenging route toward sustainable carbon utilization. However, its practical implementation is severely hindered by low selectivity and activity, primarily originating from the high energy barrier involved in the rate-limiting *C2–*C1 coupling step. Herein, we have successfully constructed an elusive *CH–*CHO coupling pathway on a stable Janus Cu2+/Cu0 catalyst, enabling low-barrier *C2 intermediate formation and highly selective n-propanol production. Leveraging the strong electron-accepting capacity of Cu2+ sites, key *CHO intermediates are strongly adsorbed and driven toward deep reduction to *CH species, effectively overcoming the critical five-electron transfer bottleneck for *CH generation. Meanwhile, adjacent Cu0 sites provide moderate and balanced adsorption of *CHO intermediates, allowing their asymmetric coupling with the Cu2+-stabilized *CH via a markedly low energy barrier, synergistically steering the reaction along the favorable *CH–*CHO pathway. In situ fiber-optic guided ATR-FTIR spectroscopy provides evidence for the coexistence of *CHO and *CHx-related intermediates, while DFT calculations further support the proposed *CH–*CHO coupling pathway. Accordingly, the Janus Cu2+/Cu0 catalyst achieves a high n-propanol Faradaic efficiency of 18.1% at a partial current density of 72.4 mA cm–2, alongside remarkable stability. This work establishes the *CH–*CHO pathway as a powerful strategy for kinetically favorable C–C coupling, opening a new mechanistic avenue for efficient conversion of CO2 to multicarbon via electrosynthesis.</jats:p>

title: Functionalized Interface Engineering of Cellulose-Based Electrolytes for Safety and Long-Life Li–Metal Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cellulose-based electrolytes are low-cost, eco-friendly solid-state electrolyte candidates owing to renewability and biodegradability. However, their flammability raises safety concerns, and crystallinity leads to low ion conduction. Herein, a dual-functionalization strategy is proposed, which grafts phytic and sulfate groups onto cellulose via a ternary deep eutectic solvent system. Phytic groups provide flame retardancy, and sulfate groups realize fast Li-ion conduction. The resulting electrolyte delivers a Li-ion conductivity (1.48 × 10–3 S cm–1) and an oxidation potential (5.2 V), and the fabricated electrolyte membrane shows a uniform structure, enhanced mechanical flexibility, and strong tensile stress. It also shows good compatibility with the Li metal, enabling stable cycling and long cycle life for solid-state Li–metal cells, including the LiFePO4 and LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 cells over 542 and 409 cycles, respectively. Moreover, this solid-state electrolyte exhibits self-extinguishing properties, helping solid-state cells work stably under extreme thermal conditions. This research offers an approach for developing safe cellulose-based electrolytes for next-generation Li–metal batteries.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Dipolar Heterointerface Enabled by Molecular Zwitterionicity for Rigid and Flexible Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Poor interfacial compatibility at the interface between the electron transport layer (ETL) and the perovskite gives rise to defect-rich interfaces with weak adhesion, representing a major critical limitation that hinders the efficiency, operational stability, and mechanical robustness of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Herein, a zwitterionic molecule, 3-(1-pyridinio)-1-propanesulfonate (Pyps), is introduced at the ETL/perovskite interface to construct a dipolar heterointerface, where the sulfonate (–SO3–) and pyridinium moieties synergistically reinforce interfacial bonding, passivate buried interfacial defects, and enhance the conductivity of the SnO2 ETL, while its large intrinsic dipole moment tailors the interfacial energy-level alignment to both improve charge extraction and suppress recombination. As a result, the dipolar heterointerface enables champion efficiencies of 26.86% and 25.50% for rigid and flexible PSCs, respectively. The unencapsulated PSCs retain over 93.2% of their initial performance under continuous operation after 1300 h, demonstrating the promise of dipolar heterointerface engineering for high-performance PSCs.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Internal Stress Effects on Electrode Stability in Coin Cells with Different Assembly Configurations
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laboratory-level evaluation of electrode materials is typically conducted using hand-assembled coin cells (half cells) with a lithium metal counter electrode. However, the lack of standardized protocols for coin cell assembly across global laboratories results in inconsistent experimental outcomes, hindering data comparability and scientific progress in battery research. Herein, through fully automated robotic assembly of cells, we systematically investigated the influence of two different yet widely adopted cell configurations (spring and spacer located on the sides of the positive electrode cap and negative electrode cap are labeled as SS-P and SS-N, respectively) on the electrode materials. Different stress distributions were found on the electrodes due to the internal structural discrepancies, leading to variations in electrochemical performance, electrode structure, and electrode–electrolyte interphase properties. This work emphasizes the critical need to raise awareness about the standardization of battery assembly protocols, enabling researchers to fabricate coin cells with high repeatability and consistency.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Prestripping Protocol for Reconciling Lithium Dissolution and Galvanic Corrosion in Anode-Free Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The practical viability of high-energy-density anode-free lithium metal batteries is limited by the poor reversibility of lithium plating and stripping. Low-current stripping suppresses pitting and inactive Li formation but prolongs electrolyte exposure and galvanic corrosion, whereas high-current stripping shortens the corrosion time but promotes localized dissolution and structural disintegration. Here, we introduce a pre-stripping protocol consisting of a brief low-current stripping step followed immediately by higher-current bulk stripping, thereby establishing a uniform initial dissolution front while limiting the duration of Li–Cu galvanic coupling. Measurements across representative electrolyte formulations identify three factors associated with the balance between morphological regulation and corrosion loss: nascent solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) passivation, longer-term corrosion tolerance, and dynamic reaction area evolution. In strongly passivating formulations, the morphological benefit of prestripping outweighs the additional corrosion loss and improves Li reversibility. The protocol was further evaluated in 1 Ah anode-free pouch cells, supporting its applicability to practical cell configurations.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Bias-Free Photoelectrochemical Valorization of Glycerol at Both Photoelectrodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Harnessing photoelectrochemical systems to upgrade biomass-derived feedstocks such as glycerol offers a sustainable route for solar-driven chemical production. Nonetheless, glycerol conversion remains limited to the photoanode in current photoelectrochemical architectures, while the cathode predominantly generates hydrogen. Here, we propose a dual-electrode glycerol conversion strategy that enables simultaneous glycerol valorization at both photoelectrodes in a bias-free photoelectrochemical cell. This is achieved by enabling oxygen reduction at a CuBi2O4-based photocathode to generate H2O2, which is subsequently converted into reactive hydroxyl radicals, thereby driving photocathodic glycerol oxidation with glyceraldehyde as an important C3 product. In parallel, a Pt-decorated oxygen-deficient TiO2 photoanode promotes glycerol oxidation primarily via photogenerated holes. The coupled system operates without an externally applied bias, achieving a combined glyceraldehyde productivity of 32.1 μmol cm−2 h−1 based on the projected device area. This work establishes a dual-photoelectrode platform for solar-driven biomass valorization through distinct reaction pathways.</jats:p>

title: Interface‐to‐Bulk Grain Regulation Enables Sb2(S,Se)3 Solar Cells Exceeding 11% Efficiency
content:
This study demonstrates an interface‐to‐bulk grain regulation strategy that delivers ultra‐large‐grain (exceeding 3 µm) Sb2(S,Se)3 solar cells with a record PCE of 11.04%. This strategy effectively passivates both the bulk deep‐level and interfacial defects, optimizes heterojunction band alignment, and suppresses non‐radiative recombination, achieving an ultralow VOC deficit of 0.483 V.








ABSTRACT
Antimony selenosulfide (Sb2(S,Se)3) represents an emerging thin‐film photovoltaic absorber owing to the excellent stability, tunable bandgap (1.1–1.7 eV), and high light absorption coefficient (> 105 cm−1). Hydrothermally deposited Sb2(S,Se)3 solar cells have broken the 10% efficiency bottleneck, yet as‐prepared Sb2(S,Se)3 films suffer from small grains (typically ∼400 nm) with abundant grain boundaries (GBs) that introduce dense defect states, inducing severe non‐radiative recombination and hindering further efficiency enhancement. Here we develop an interface‐to‐bulk grain regulation strategy to achieve ultra‐large (exceeding 3 µm) columnar grains spanning the entire absorber. This strategy combines buried‐interface Sb pre‐deposition to tailor initial hydrothermal deposition and rear‐interface Se‐mediated two‐step post‐annealing to drive grain coalescence and growth through a sequential infiltration‐reaction‐coalescence mechanism. We also found that this grain engineering also leads to the passivation of bulk deep‐level and interfacial defects, and optimized heterojunction band alignment, which collectively suppresses non‐radiative recombination and in turn delivers an ultralow open‐circuit voltage deficit of 0.483 V. Consequently, the ultra‐large‐grain Sb2(S,Se)3 solar cell delivers a champion power conversion efficiency of 11.04%, which is the highest efficiency ever reported for antimony chalcogenide‐based solar cells. This study establishes an integrated strategy for regulating grain growth in Sb2(S,Se)3 films toward efficient devices.

title: Broadband Aeolian Vibration Harvesting and Electrical‐Damping‐Induced Suppression via Triboelectric‐Electromagnetic Coupling Mechanism
content:
A strategy based on a triboelectric–electromagnetic coupling mechanism is proposed to integrate broadband aeolian vibration energy harvesting with vibration suppression of transmission lines. By converting vibration energy into electricity and harnessing the associated electrical damping, this strategy enables simultaneous vibration control and self‐powered wireless sensing.








ABSTRACT
Overhead transmission lines have long faced dual threats: a scarcity of power for sensor nodes and fatigue caused by aeolian vibrations. To address these issues, this paper proposes a synergistic strategy that integrates energy harvesting with vibration suppression, transforming vibration energy dissipation into a coupled process of electrical energy conversion and vibration suppression. Based on this strategy, a triboelectric‐electromagnetic coupling device (TECD) is developed. By leveraging the complementary frequency‐domain characteristics of triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) and electromagnetic generators (EMGs), as well as the electrical damping generated during the energy conversion process, the device achieves deep synergy between wideband energy harvesting and vibration suppression. Experimental results demonstrate that the TECD can stably charge a 47 µF capacitor to a 5.2 V supply threshold at any frequency within the 5–50 Hz range, reaching a peak output power of up to 287.28 mW. Simultaneously, the associated electrical damping effectively suppresses vibrations, reducing the vibration acceleration of the primary structure by 86% under 30 Hz excitation. Built upon this device, an integrated harvesting‐suppression‐sensing system is constructed, paving a new path for self‐powered state monitoring and structural protection of transmission lines.

title: Direct Solar Storage and On‐Demand Power via Threshold‐Matched Silicon Photovoltaics and Dual‐Ion Batteries
content:
Direct coupling of silicon photovoltaics with a dual‐ion battery creates an energy‐autonomous platform that combines solar harvesting, rapid storage, and on‐demand power delivery. The system achieves 11,430 W kg−1 and 40.8 mA cm−2, reaching a high‐current regime not usually targeted by energy‐oriented lithium‐ion, lithium‐metal and all‐solid‐state pouch cells, while threshold‐based power management supports self‐sustained operation and transient high‐power demands of unmanned aerial vehicles.








ABSTRACT
Direct integration of photovoltaics with batteries is attractive for energy‐autonomous mobile platforms, but mismatched photovoltaic output and battery charging requirements, limited high‐rate capability, and low‐temperature degradation can necessitate intermediate power electronics and restrict burst‐power delivery. Here, a threshold‐matched silicon photovoltaic–dual‐ion battery (PV–DIB) architecture is demonstrated by directly coupling a voltage‐ and current‐tailored crystalline‐silicon photovoltaic module with a high‐voltage dual‐ion battery pouch cell. Under one‐sun illumination, the photovoltaic module supplies ≈72 mA at the battery charging threshold, enabling direct charging without intermediate power‐conversion hardware. This matching establishes two complementary operating regimes: solar‐sustained operation when photovoltaic current meets the load demand and on‐demand battery assistance when the load exceeds the photovoltaic input. The integrated system delivers a maximum power density of 11,430 W kg−1 at 40.83 mA cm−2, maintains stable operation under drone‐relevant dynamic load profiles, and the DIB retains 5,088 W kg−1 at −10°C. Indoor and outdoor flight demonstrations validate direct solar energy storage and burst‐power delivery, establishing threshold matching as a practical design strategy for power‐electronics‐minimized, energy‐autonomous mobile systems.

title: Synergistic Interfacial and Subsurface Stabilization of O3‐Type Na‐Ni‐Fe‐Mn‐O Cathodes through Integrated Zr Modification
content:
Zr‐treatment transforms residual sodium species on O3‐type Na[Ni0.3Fe0.3Mn0.4]O2 into a Na2ZrO3‐rich surface while introducing limited near‐surface Zr. The coupled architecture scavenges HF, suppresses cathode–electrolyte interphase growth and transition‐metal dissolution, mitigates anisotropic lattice variation, and enables 61.8% capacity retention after 500 cycles in hard‐carbon full cells under prolonged high‐voltage operation.








ABSTRACT
Surface degradation, electrolyte‐derived hydrogen fluoride (HF) attack, and anisotropic phase evolution limit the stability of O3‐type sodium cathodes. An integrated Zr‐based surface/subsurface strategy is developed for Na[Ni0.3Fe0.3Mn0.4]O2 (NFM). Treatment at 800°C converts residual Na2CO3/NaOH into a Na2ZrO3‐rich surface nanolayer, accompanied by limited near‐surface Zr incorporation. In hard‐carbon full cells, NFM‐Zr‐800 delivers ∼150 mAh g−1 with ∼87% initial Coulombic efficiency and retains 61.8% capacity after 500 cycles at 0.5 C, compared with 26.4% for bare NFM. Operando X‐ray diffraction shows reduced anisotropic lattice variation during the P3‐to‐OP2 transition. X‐ray absorption spectroscopy, Mössbauer spectroscopy, and hybrid‐functional calculations indicate Ni/Fe‐dominated cationic redox, nearly tetravalent Mn, and no major lattice‐oxygen redox contribution. Coulomb–Buckingham calculations suggest that Zr incorporation at Mn sites is energetically favored near the surface within the adopted model. The Na2ZrO3‐rich layer mitigates HF‐related interfacial degradation and promotes a Zr–F‐containing protective interface, suppressing transition‐metal dissolution, cathode–electrolyte interphase thickening, particle cracking, and surface reconstruction. These coupled interfacial and structural effects improve the long‐term stability of O3‐type NFM cathodes.

title: Operando Pressure Monitoring, EIS, and X‐Ray Imaging of Solid‐State Sodium‐Sulfur Batteries — Insights into Chemo‐Mechanical Degradation Mechanisms
content:
A multi‐modal operando platform combining pressure monitoring, impedance spectroscopy, and X‐ray imaging reveals degradation pathways in solid‐state Na||S batteries with sulfide‐based electrolytes. While Na3PS4 promotes localized Na plating‐like behavior and dendrite growth, chloride content in a multiphase electrolyte suppresses these effects. These findings highlight the power of advanced operando diagnostics for advancing the development of durable and resource‐abundant solid‐state batteries.








ABSTRACT
In this study, we introduce a multi‐modal operando platform that combines cell stack pressure monitoring, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and x‐ray imaging to unravel the chemo‐mechanical aging processes in sulfide‐based solid‐state sodium‐sulfur (ssNa||S) cells. Despite their promising theoretical capacity and resource abundance, the mechanisms that limit the full performance of ssNa||S batteries are still poorly understood. To address this issue, we employ a new multi‐modal operando setup optimized for solid‐state cells. By comparing cells with different electrolytes, Na3PS4 (NPS), a multiphase electrolyte Na2S‐P2S5‐NaCl (NPS‐Cl), and Na3SbS4 (NSbS), operando over the course of 50 cycles, we monitor slowly evolving aging effects that are found to be correlated with the electrolyte composition. For NPS, the combination of low interfacial stability against sodium and reduced ionic conductivity causes the electrochemical activity to be concentrated in localized regions, leading to sodium plating‐like behavior as the dominant degradation mechanism. In contrast, the chloride‐containing NPS‐Cl enhances the interfacial stability and mitigates dendrite formation. These findings provide valuable insights for the materials development of sulfide‐based electrolytes for ssNa||S cells and demonstrate the capability of combined operando diagnostics to resolve complex chemo‐mechanical phenomena that influence solid‐state battery performance.

title: Directed Perovskite‐to‐Fullerene Electron Shuttle for 27.2% Inverted Solar Cells
content:
A pyridinium‐based interfacial modulator, PPTHI, is synthesized to address the weak contact and conduction band mismatch between perovskite and C60. By anchoring to halide vacancies and facilitating electron shuttling, PPTHI improves electron extraction and energy level alignment. This strategy delivers a certified stabilized efficiency of 26.54% (27.2% champion cell) and retains over 80% of initial efficiency after 2000 h of maximum power point tracking.








ABSTRACT
Although C60 is almost exclusively used in the electron transport layers of high‐performance inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs), its weak affinity and unfavorable energy level alignment with perovskite lead to weak contact and mismatch in the conduction band level at the perovskite/C60 interface, thereby limiting further improvement of device efficiency as well as compromising device long‐term operational stability. We synthesized an n‐type Pyridinium molecule, 2,7‐di(pyridin‐4‐yl)benzo[lmn][3,8]phenanthroline‐1,3,6,8(2H,7H)‐tetraone dihydroiodide (PPTHI), and used it as the interfacial electron‐selective contact in inverted PSCs. The pyridinium iodide head unit in the PPTHI anchored to the halide vacancies and coordinated with the exposed lead. Moreover, the π‐conjugated core renders desirable electron‐transport capability, and the n‐type interfacial modulator can also serve as an electron shuttle between perovskite and the C60 electron transport layer. The improved electron extraction, optimized energetic, and passivated top surface translated to reduced VOC losses, leading to a certified stabilized power output efficiency of 26.54% and a champion device with an efficiency of 27.2% and a fill factor of 87.17%. Moreover, inverted PSCs incorporating the electron shuttle maintained over 80% of their initial efficiency after 2000 h of maximum power point tracking.

title: Polyanion‐Modulated Vanadium‐Doped Ammonium Iron Phosphate Framework from Spent LiFePO4 for Lattice Oxygen‐Participated Water Oxidation
content:
Microwave‐assisted upcycling converts spent LiFePO4 into S‐VAFP featuring a three‐dimensional polyanionic framework. The framework modulates Fe─O bonding and promotes surface reconstruction, enhancing lattice oxygen participation during the oxygen evolution reaction. S‐VAFP exhibits an overpotential of 250 mV at 100 mA cm−2. The AEMWE cell achieves 1.72 V at 1 A cm−2 and remains stable for over 1000 h.








ABSTRACT
Promoting the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM) offers an effective route to improving the efficiency of water electrolysis. However, achieving efficient LOM operation in structurally stable catalysts remains challenging. To address this challenge, we report a microwave‐assisted upcycling strategy using spent LiFePO4 as a lithium‐deficient precursor. The cycling‐induced lithium deficiency facilitates structural reorganization into a polyanion‐modulated vanadium‐doped ammonium iron phosphate hydroxide hydrate (S‐VAFP) without residual Li‐containing impurities. The resulting S‐VAFP features a three‐dimensional polyanionic framework composed of FeO6 octahedra vertex‐linked with PO4 tetrahedra, forming one‐dimensional channels that promote electrolyte accessibility and ion transport. This architecture tunes Fe─O covalency, weakens Fe─(O─P) linkages, and drives in situ reconstruction into a catalytically active amorphous phase, thereby facilitating lattice oxygen participation. Chemical probe experiments and 18O isotope‐labeling DEMS further verify the AEM–LOM coupled OER pathway. Benefiting from this structure‐guided LOM activation, S‐VAFP delivers an overpotential of 250 mV at 100 mA cm−2 with a Tafel slope of 47.2 mV dec‒1. An assembled anion‐exchange membrane water electrolyzer (AEMWE) cell achieves 1.72 V at 1 A cm−2 with stability exceeding 1000 h. Overall, this work establishes polyanion‐mediated electronic modulation as an effective strategy for designing stable iron phosphate electrocatalysts with enhanced lattice oxygen participation.

title: Thiophenol‐Catalyzed Anti‐Markovnikov Coupling of α‐Methylene‐γ‐Butenolides Under Visible Light: Total Synthesis of Aucklappalide A
content:
Visible‐light thiophenol catalysis enables the first anti‐Markovnikov intermolecular coupling of α‐methylene‐γ‐butenolides under photocatalyst‐free conditions. A sulfur‐mediated photochemical manifold involving a competent thiophenol adduct promotes intermolecular C–C bond formation, providing concise access to complex disesquiterpenoid architectures, including aucklappalide A.








ABSTRACT
General methods for the selective anti‐Markovnikov intermolecular coupling of electron‐poor alkenes remain scarce. Herein, we report a visible‐light‐mediated, photocatalyst‐free strategy for the anti‐Markovnikov coupling of α‐methylene‐γ‐butenolides using a simple formate/thiophenol reaction platform. The method enables the direct synthesis of structurally diverse homo‐ and cross‐coupled disesquiterpenoid architectures from complex sesquiterpenoid lactones, including the first total synthesis of aucklappalide A. Mechanistic investigations support a distinct sulfur‐mediated photochemical manifold involving a thiophenol adduct that provides access to the carbon‐centered radical required for intermolecular C–C bond formation. These findings establish a photocatalyst‐free approach to the redox‐neutral anti‐Markovnikov coupling of α‐methylene‐γ‐butenolides, uncover a previously unrecognized sulfur‐mediated radical manifold enabled by formate/thiophenol photochemistry, and suggest that related sulfur‐centered radical processes may contribute to the biosynthesis of dimeric sesquiterpenoid lactones.

title: Catalytically Active Species and Sites in CO2 Hydrogenation Identified by Modulation Excitation Spectroscopy
content:
Rational design of better catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation requires detailed knowledge of the reaction mechanism including key intermediates and active sites. This Minireview discusses the potential of modulation excitation spectroscopy as a powerful tool to identify active species and sites as illustrated by the current literature, and gives an outlook on methodical extentions and applications beyond thermal catalysis.








ABSTRACT
Thermocatalytic carbon dioxide (CO2) hydrogenation has developed into an important sustainable route toward valuable fuels and chemicals, thereby reducing the greenhouse gas CO2 and supporting the energy transition. For a rational design of more efficient, selective, and stable catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation, detailed knowledge of the reaction mechanism, including key intermediates and active sites is required. Modulation excitation spectroscopy (MES) has emerged as a powerful tool to discriminate between catalytically active and (nonparticipating) spectator species and to identify active sites, and has been shown to provide important new mechanistic findings not accessible by steady‐state approaches, contributing to the very intense debate on CO2 hydrogenation mechanisms. Despite its broad applicability, the MES method is still rarely used in catalysis research and has contributed to the mechanism of CO2 hydrogenation mainly by its combination with infrared spectroscopy. In this Minireview, the potential of MES for providing mechanistic insight on catalytic CO2 hydrogenation will be illustrated based on the current literature, followed by an outline of potential methodical extensions. Future prospects for the application of MES to mechanistic studies on CO2 activation beyond thermal catalysis, including photo‐ and electrocatalysis, as well as other areas of research will be discussed.

title: Guide DNAs Program Enzyme for Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA Without Target Denaturation and Amplification
content:
Chemically modified guide DNAs program λ exonuclease to access native double‐stranded ctDNA at room temperature, enabling detection without target amplification or denaturation. Coupling this chemistry to a DNAzyme and single‐molecule fluorescence readout supports sensitive EGFR L858R ctDNA analysis in plasma.








ABSTRACT
Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is fragmented, tumor‐derived cell‐free double‐stranded DNA (dsDNA) whose low abundance and limited sequence accessibility complicate detection under mild conditions. Here we show that guide DNAs (gDNAs) can program an exonuclease to interrogate native dsDNA under mild conditions and convert this access into a single‐molecule fluorescence readout. We found that gDNA 5′‐terminal chemistry regulates λ exonuclease (λExo) recruitment. Among those termini, anionic 5′‐phosphate and 5′‐carboxyl‐C10 phosphate enabled the strongest target‐dependent processing. Molecular simulations suggested a possible structural basis for these activity differences based on terminal positioning within the catalytic pocket. Coupling the optimized 5′‐carboxyl‐C10 phosphate gDNA with 10–23 DNAzyme turnover generated a single‐molecule fluorescence readout without target nucleic‐acid amplification. The assay detected dsDNA down to 10 fM across 10–1000 fM, showed a statistically significant response at an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) L858R mutant fraction of 0.05% under the tested conditions, and was applied to 24 plasma samples (12 from patients with non‐small‐cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and 12 from healthy donors), achieving 91.7% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 95.8% accuracy, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of 0.97. This work establishes gDNA‐programmed enzyme access as a route for detecting low‐abundance duplex tumor DNA.

title: Confinement Enables Direct Electrosynthesis of Acetaldoxime From CO and Nitrate
content:
We report a confinement‐enhanced electrocatalytic route for acetaldoxime synthesis from CO and NO3− via C–N coupling. By encapsulating ultrasmall Cu nanoparticles into SBA‐15, the sluggish C–C dimerization is kinetically matched with rapid NO3− reduction, favoring the oximation pathway and achieving a production rate of 255.1 mmol gcat.−1 h−1 with an 8.2% Faradaic efficiency, enabling sustainable co‐upcycling of carbon and nitrogen wastes.








ABSTRACT
Aldoximes are vital feedstocks in the fields of medicine, agriculture, and industry, yet their conventional synthesis suffers from high environmental costs and carbon footprints. Here, we report a direct electrocatalytic route to acetaldoxime via CO and NO3− co‐reduction. The C–N coupling efficiency in this process hinges on the kinetic match between CO reduction and NO3− reduction. Acetaldoxime synthesis exemplifies this challenge: sluggish C–C dimerization contrasts with rapid NO3−RR, leading to over‐reduction of nitrogen species to NH3. We hypothesized that a confinement strategy could selectively promote C–C dimerization and enrich acetaldehyde intermediate, thereby facilitating oximation. Ultrasmall Cu nanoparticles were encapsulated within SBA‐15 mesopores to selectively accelerate the dimerization step. Combined operando Raman and in situ differential electrochemical mass spectrometry reveal that the confined Cu lowers the overpotential for the key C2 intermediate to align with that for NH2OH generation, enabling efficient C–N coupling to acetaldoxime. The optimized Cu@SBA‐15 catalyst achieves an acetaldoxime production rate of 255.1 mmol gcat.−1 h−1 (partial current density: 24.6 mA cm−2). This work establishes a sustainable pathway toward aldoximes, aligning with green chemistry principles while expanding the toolbox for electrocatalytic C–N bond formation.

title: Phase and Conformational Transitions in Biomolecules and Polymers With Nanopores
content:
Nanopore sensing provides a powerful electrical method for probing the phase transitions of biological macromolecules and polymers. This review explores how confined nanoscale environments enable direct, single‐molecule observation of protein unfolding, biomolecular aggregation, DNA unzipping, and polymer collapse. These fundamental insights drive forward early biomarker detection and the next generation of molecular sequencing technologies. 








ABSTRACT
Phase transitions have been studied extensively for a long time, both experimentally and theoretically, to understand physical, chemical, and biological processes. Here, we focus mainly on biological molecules for which changes in state or conformation are correlated with their biological function, pathological implications, or potential biotechnology applications. We discuss how a nanohole, or a nanopore, with electrical detection could detect and characterize the phase transition of biological macromolecules in confined media. We illustrate the review with emblematic molecules of life: nucleic acids and proteins. We discuss DNA and RNA denaturation, their compaction and decompaction; we also discuss protein folding using different approaches, denaturing agents, electric forces, molecular motors, and their aggregation. Finally, we present polymer phase transitions or conformational modifications to characterize polymer size or detect biomarkers. The studies presented here are discussed in comparison with other single‐molecule approaches. We also discuss the potential contributions of nanopore approaches to resolving biological questions or to applications.

title: Microstructure‐Regulated Electrochemical Doping Enables High‐Performance Organic Thermoelectrics
content:
Microstructure‐regulated electrochemical doping integrates potential‐controlled carrier generation with PDA‐directed crystallization in PBTTT, creating ordered pathways for charge transport. The resulting films reach a power factor of 264.8 µW m−1 K−2 while exhibiting improved electrical stability, which supports their reliable use in wireless wristband temperature monitoring with smartphone readout and threshold alerts.








ABSTRACT
Efficient and stable doping of conjugated polymers is critical for high‐performance organic thermoelectrics and reliable wearable temperature monitoring. However, increasing carrier density often disrupts molecular organization, thereby limiting charge transport and inducing electrical drift. This work develops a microstructure‐regulated electrochemical doping strategy using poly[2,5‐bis(3‐tetradecylthiophen‐2‐yl)thieno[3,2‐b]thiophene] (PBTTT) and N,N′‐(1,4‐phenylene)diisonicotinamide (PDA) as a nucleating agent. Electrochemical oxidation enables controllable carrier generation, while PDA regulates PBTTT crystallization and molecular packing to create ordered transport pathways. The optimized PBTTT/PDA film exhibits an electrical conductivity of 1044 S cm−1, a Seebeck coefficient of 50.3 µV K−1, and a power factor of 264.8 µW m−1 K−2, more than three times that of electrochemically doped PBTTT without PDA. Similar enhancement is observed in three additional conjugated‐polymer systems, supporting the broader applicability of the strategy. PDA incorporation also suppresses storage‐induced resistance drift, supporting reliable use in wearable devices. Leveraging its temperature‐dependent resistance, the film shows a linear negative temperature coefficient response from 25°C to 40°C and enables real‐time wireless temperature monitoring and threshold alerts in a flexible wristband. These results demonstrate that coordinated control of doping level and molecular organization provides an effective route toward high thermoelectric performance and stable wearable temperature monitoring.

title: Thermal Dynamics as a Non‐Invasive Indicator for Cycle Life Prediction of LiFePO4/Graphite Batteries Under Fast‐Charging
content:
A temperature‐based prognostic approach to enable early prediction of battery cycle life, focusing on the thermal response of LiFePO4/graphite cells subjected to fast‐charging protocols.








ABSTRACT
Resistance‐induced overpotential and the associated heat generation are critical factors affecting cycle life of lithium‐ion batteries under fast‐charging conditions. In this study, we propose a temperature‐based prognostic approach for the early prediction of battery cycle life, focusing on LiFePO4/graphite cells cycled under a fixed family of multistep fast‐charging protocols at 30°C. The charging process was segmented into four state‐of‐charge (SoC)‐resolved constant‐current regions (CC1–CC4). Voltage and temperature analyses revealed that the initial SoC region (CC1) is particularly sensitive to overpotential development, where a high current density is associated with a premature transition to the constant‐voltage (CV) mode and intensified heat generation. At advanced stages of cycling, temperature behavior exhibited correlations with cycle life consistent with voltage responses. Based on these observations, temperature evolution during the early cycles (third to 10th) was employed to construct a cycle life prediction model. Among the CC‐resolved regions, temperature‐related features from CC1 and CC4 showed higher predictive relevance than those from CC2 and CC3. These results suggest that non‐invasively measured surface temperature can serve as a physically meaningful indicator for early‐stage cycle life prognosis under the studied fast‐charging conditions. The proposed framework provides an interpretable approach for battery health monitoring and fast‐charging protocol design.

title:
G:C:G:C-Flanked i-Motifs
Are Thermodynamically
Favored and Their Sequences Highly Enriched in the Human Genome
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>i-Motifs are biologically relevant noncanonical DNA structures whose stability is strongly influenced by capping interactions. Among these, minor groove tetrads (MGTs) are among the most powerful stabilizing elements identified to date, yet the molecular factors governing their effects and their potential biological significance remain poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic experimental and computational analysis of 16 MGT-stabilized i-motifs (MGTiMs), encompassing all combinations of terminal tetrad composition and orientation within a common sequence scaffold. NMR spectroscopy confirms that all sequences adopt closely related architectures, enabling direct comparison of the effects of tetrad identity and orientation on stability. Thermal denaturation experiments reveal that the stability hierarchy, previously observed in selected structures (G:C:G:C ≳ G:C:G:T ≫ G:T:G:T), is broadly maintained across the series, although substantial positional effects are observed. Molecular dynamics simulations and energy decomposition analyses suggest that differences in electrostatic interactions and local conformational flexibility contribute to these trends. Notably, genome-wide analysis of the human genome reveals a strong enrichment of sequences capable of forming the most stabilizing tetrads, with motifs containing two G:C:G:C tetrads reaching a 45-fold enrichment relative to random expectation. Interestingly, this most abundant genomic motif is also the only one that undergoes pronounced pH-driven conformational transitions, highlighting the unique structural plasticity of these architectures. Together, these findings reveal how tetrad composition and positional context govern MGTiM stability and identify NN-type motifs as a particularly enriched class of structurally distinctive genomic sequences.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Radical Ring-Opening Polymerization of endo -Cyclic Monomers for Regioregularity Control in Vinyl Polymers
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Radical polymerization of vinyl monomers is inherently governed by propagation pathways that favor head-to-tail connectivity, limiting access to alternative backbone regioregularities. To address this challenge, we report the radical ring-opening polymerization (rROP) of endo-cyclic monomers, a class of monomers that has been largely unexplored in radical processes. Whereas many established rROP systems have been designed to introduce functional or cleavable units into polymer backbones, the present endo-cyclic monomers undergo selective rROP to generate carbon–carbon-backboned vinyl polymers enriched with nonhead-to-tail linkages. Copolymerization with conventional vinyl monomers was also achieved, providing access to copolymers with tunable backbone microstructures. In particular, using vinyl ketones and their corresponding endo-cyclic cyclodimers as structurally matched pairs, we accessed poly(vinyl ketone)s with systematically varied head-to-tail linkage contents. This control over backbone regioregularity translated into tunable macroscopic properties, including glass transition temperature and photodegradation kinetics, establishing regioregularity as a structural handle for controlling material properties. The strategy was also compatible with controlled radical polymerization, enabling the synthesis of well-defined block copolymers. Micelles assembled from these block copolymers further exhibited regioregularity-dependent sizes and photoresponsive behavior. These findings establish endo-cyclic rROP as a previously unrecognized strategy for controlling backbone regioregularity and properties in vinyl polymers.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
NMR Reveals Coupled
Ligand and Protein Conformational
Equilibria That Modulate the Affinity of MDM2-Inhibitory Peptoids
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Peptoids, atypical peptides with N-substitutions, are a promising drug modality for targeting protein–protein interactions. The binding affinity of an MDM2-inhibitory peptoid decreases by more than 100-fold upon removal of the backbone-restricting methyl groups attached to the α-carbons, although this modification alters the population of the all-trans amide-bond isomer by only 1.6-fold. This discrepancy raises the possibility that backbone flexibility affects not only ligand preorganization but also the conformational ensemble of the target protein. Here, we used NMR to examine the binding mode of the MDM2-peptoid complexes. ZZ-exchange experiments demonstrated that peptoid isomers containing cis amide bonds bind less favorably to MDM2 than the all-trans amide bond isomer. In addition, observation of the I19 δ1-methyl resonance of MDM2 in complex with the peptoids revealed that MDM2 exists in equilibrium between an open state, corresponding to the crystal structure of the MDM2-peptoid complex, and a semiclosed state, which retains partial interactions between the N-terminal region of MDM2 and the ligand-binding cleft. Increased population of the semiclosed state correlated with reduced binding affinities of the peptoids. We propose that cis-trans isomerization of the peptoid amide bonds and the conformational equilibrium of MDM2 within the peptoid complex synergistically contribute to the more than 100-fold decrease in binding affinity. These results identify coupled ligand and protein conformational equilibria as determinants of binding affinity and suggest conformational-plasticity control as a potential design principle for oligomeric ligands targeting protein–protein interactions.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
Experimental and Computational
Identification of Wide-Gap
Quaternary Oxychalcogenides BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Oxychalcogenides have attracted attention as candidates for wide-gap p-type semiconductors in view of the energetically high and spatially spread characteristics of their valence electronic states. An appropriate choice of constituent cations would also enable n-type doping. However, reports on p-type doping have been mostly limited to Cu-based systems, which exhibit a strong p-type tendency due to hole generation and electron compensation by native Cu-vacancy acceptors. Oxychalcogenides with a practical level of n-type conductivity are yet to be developed. In this study, we focus on oxychalcogenides in the Ae–Zn–O–Ch (Ae = Ca, Sr, Ba; Ch = S, Se) quaternary system to explore new wide-gap semiconductors. Two as-yet-unreported compounds with wide band gaps, namely BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2, have been synthesized, along with four previously reported oxychalcogenides. First-principles calculations indicate that both BaZn2OS2 and SrZn2OSe2 feature direct-type band structures with low electron and hole effective masses, comparable to related compounds. Carrier compensation by native defects, however, is likely to make BaZn2OS2 insulating, whereas it can be well suppressed in SrZn2OSe2 by controlling the growth conditions. Systematic calculations of extrinsic dopants predict that bipolar doping of SrZn2OSe2 is feasible. Our results reveal the potential of non-Cu-based oxychalcogenides as a platform for the development of wide-gap, bipolar-dopable semiconductors, thereby stimulating exploration of related compounds.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
Direct-to-Biology Bifunctional
Screening Reveals Noncanonical
Mechanisms of Targeted Protein Degradation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a powerful strategy for modulating protein function through small-molecule-induced proximity between a protein of interest (POI) and typically an E3 ubiquitin ligase to promote its proteasomal degradation. Despite significant progress, most degraders co-opt a narrow set of E3 ubiquitin ligases, motivating mechanistically agnostic strategies for discovering new routes to degradation. Here, we pursued a “degrader-first” approach using direct-to-biology (D2B) synthesis to construct and screen a 114-member library of BRD4-targeting bifunctional molecules to identify chemically tractable ligases that support TPD. Multiple compounds were found to induce Cullin-RING ligase (CRL)-dependent degradation, and two top hits were selected for mechanistic characterization. Unexpectedly, neither operates through canonical heterobifunctional E3 recruitment. Instead, one undergoes oxidative activation to generate a reactive electrophile that promotes degradation through DCAF11- or DCAF16-containing CRL4 complexes in a cell-context-dependent manner. The second acts through a bivalent bromodomain-binding mechanism that likely induces target conformational contraction and potentiates endogenous CRL3–SPOP-mediated ubiquitination. These findings highlight the capacity of D2B discovery approaches to expose noncanonical modalities of TPD while underscoring the importance of rigorous mechanistic deconvolution in interpreting screening-derived degraders.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
Halogenated
Triazole-Based Metal–Organic Framework
Achieves Ultra-Selective CO2 Capture under Humid Conditions
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Selective CO2 capture from humid, N2-rich flue gas requires adsorbents that combine extreme CO2/N2 discrimination with robustness under realistic conditions. However, only a few MOFs are able to combine ultrahigh selectivity, humidity tolerance, scalable synthesis, and structural durability. Here, we introduce CALF-20-X (X = Cl or Br) halogentriazolate–oxalate Zn-MOFs and a PVDF composite, integrating these attributes into an ultramicroporous framework. The halogenated Zn-MOFs are obtained by means of solvent-minimized liquid-assisted grinding followed by water-incubation route, producing a highly crystalline material. Halogen functionalization polarizes the triazolate C–H donor, thereby promoting directional C–H···O(CO2) contacts and enhancing electrostatic complementarity, as evidenced by an experimental isosteric heat of adsorption of 48 kJ/mol. Furthermore, this halogen substitution significantly restricts the size of the pore window inhibiting N2 uptake, and leads to the formation of perfectly CO2-fitted pockets. These combined features enabled a CO2 excellent adsorption of 2.89 mmol g–1 at 0.15 bar and 298 K, and CO2/N2 selectivity higher than 4074 for CALF-20-Cl, exceeding leading physisorbent benchmarks. The highly selective CO2 capture was confirmed by dynamic breakthrough experiments performed on a CALF-20-Cl@PVDF composite under humid conditions over numerous cycles, thus demonstrating its robust performance under flue-gas-relevant conditions. Competitive CO2/H2O breakthrough experiments, supported by GCMC simulations, demonstrate that CO2 sorption is favored at 21% relative humidity (RH), resulting in a 56% suppression of water uptake, and even remains competitive at RH &gt; 50% and 318 K, a temperature relevant for carbon capture from point sources. These results highlight halogen-driven structural engineering for regenerable and humidity-tolerant next-generation CO2-selective MOF adsorbents with complete retention of the performance metrics.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
Catalytic Enantiodivergent
Neophyl Rearrangement
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The neophyl rearrangement is a long-established radical 1,2-aryl migration, yet catalytic enantioselective control of this process has remained elusive. Here we report a cooperative photoredox and chiral Brønsted acid catalytic system for the enantioselective neophyl rearrangement of tertiary alcohol-derived olefins. The reaction affords 1,5-dicarbonyl compounds bearing azaarene-substituted all-carbon quaternary stereocenters with up to 97% ee. Changing the radical precursor alters the preferred mode of catalyst recognition and reverses the absolute stereochemical outcome with the same catalyst configuration, providing access to opposite product enantiomers. The reaction also accommodates racemic olefin substrates, and experiments with the individual substrate enantiomers show that the chiral catalyst can counter their intrinsic stereochemical preferences. The results reveal how changes in catalyst–substrate recognition can alter stereochemical control during a transient radical rearrangement.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
Resolving Chlorine
Sites in Pharmaceuticals by Integrated
Site-Resolved Zeeman-Perturbed NQR, Solid-State NMR, and Electron
Diffraction Crystallography
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Many active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and high-value chemicals feature covalently bonded chlorine functionalities that influence molecular packing, stability, and bioavailability. However, site-resolved structural characterization of chlorine sites in powders remains challenging, especially in systems with multiple chemically or crystallographically nonequivalent sites, disorder, or hydration sensitivity. We report here a novel combined 35Cl nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR), 35Cl Zeeman-perturbed NQR (Zp-NQR), 35Cl solid-state NMR, and three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED/microcrystal electron diffraction) approach to characterizing powdered chlorine-bearing chemicals. Case studies of ketoconazole and chloramine-T demonstrate the utility of the approach in characterizing local structural heterogeneity and the hydration state. The role of crystal packing and noncovalent interactions on the spectroscopic observables is provided through an analysis of chlorzoxazone and five of its cocrystals, of which three are novel. Compared to ultrahigh-field NMR spectra alone, NQR and Zp-NQR spectra provide improved sensitivity to small changes in the electric field gradient and in the degree of disorder around chlorine. Experimental NQR/Zp-NQR data combined with gauge-including projector augmented-wave density functional theory (GIPAW-DFT) provide local structural constraints for a partially dehydrated chloramine-T phase. The refinement protocol does not require single crystals, and in the case of NQR experiments, intact tablets containing APIs are analyzed directly without further treatment or grinding. As a proof of principle, commercial tablets are shown to contain ketoconazole in the same crystalline form as that seen for the pure API. The general approach could be extended to other complex solids incorporating quadrupolar nuclei and is not limited to solid-form screening, polymorph identification, and differentiation of salts and cocrystals.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
Nanoscale Flexibility
Enables Low-Enthalpy Cooperative
Water Sorption
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Passive, sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting technologies (AWHTs) have attracted recent interest as an alternative to energy-intensive condensation-based technologies. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) offer wide chemical tunability to design sorbents, but in practice, sorbents must retain moisture during humidity fluctuations, and small adsorption enthalpies are necessary for regeneration of the sorbent material. Here, we report that Cu(1,2,3-triazolate)2 nanoparticles with diameters less than 120 nm exhibit structural flexibility at the Cu2+ centers that enables a “breathing”-type cooperative water sorption. This cooperative structural phase change occurs only for nanoparticles that contain Cu2+, and not for the isomorphic magnesium triazolate. The phase change significantly decreases the onset pressures of adsorption and desorption compared to large particles and opens a practically useful hysteresis window in the isotherms, while maintaining small adsorption enthalpies (48 kJ/mol averaged over the isotherm, approaching the 44 kJ/mol latent heat of water at low RH). Mechanistic analysis indicates that adsorption initiates with weak electrostatic and dispersion interactions between water and triazolate rings brought into close proximity only by the distorted Cu2+ centers of the nanoparticles. Together, these results present a distinct water sorption mechanism and design strategy that leverages size- and metal-dependent lattice flexibility in a wide class of porous materials.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
Entropy Engineering
Accelerates High-Temperature Oxygen
Evolution Reaction Rate via Spin Manipulation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The high-temperature oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity is closely correlated to the spin state of transition metals in perovskite anodes. However, the roles of entropy engineering in modulating the spin state and influencing high-temperature OER kinetics remain poorly understood. Herein, we demonstrate that entropy engineering of La0.7Sr0.3FeO3−δ to (SmNdPrLaBaSrCa)FeO3−δ (SNPLBSCF) induces a transition of B-site Fe species from high-spin to low-spin states. This transition enhances the d–p hybridization of Fe–O bonds, lowers the energy barriers for electron transfer and oxygen ion migration, and finally accelerates the high-temperature OER kinetics. Consequently, the SNPLBSCF anode in a solid oxide electrolysis cell (SOEC) achieves a current density of 3.64 A·cm–2 at 800 °C and 1.6 V, outperforming most reported anodes. This work not only provides fundamental insights into the spin state-activity relationships of perovskite oxides but also offers a viable strategy for the rational design of highly efficient SOEC anodes through entropy engineering.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Chemical Programming of Stacking Order and Superconductivity Dimensionality in NbSe 2–x Te x Polytypic Heterostructures
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Layered transition-metal dichalcogenides exhibit electronic states highly sensitive to lattice symmetry, yet elucidating the structure–superconductivity relationship has been challenging due to the lack of a continuous structural evolution within a single material system. Here, we establish NbSe2–xTex as a model system, where Te substitution drives a sequential polytypic transition across the full composition range─from the low-Te 2H phase, through mixed 1H/1T heterostructured 4H and 6R polytypes at intermediate substitution, to ideal 1T and distorted 1T′ structures at high Te content. Combining comprehensive characterizations, we map both the structural evolution and the accompanying changes in spectral weight and orbital character near the Fermi level. Electrical transport measurements reveal a striking phase-dependent superconducting dimensionality: the 4H phase (NbSe1.4Te0.6) exhibits enhanced anisotropy and an anomalous boost in the in-plane upper critical field, while the 6R phase (NbSe1.2Te0.8) shows suppressed Tc (∼2.8 K) and three-dimensional-like behavior. The combined electronic-structure and superconducting results connect the stacking sequence to effective interlayer coherence and the local spin–orbit environment. SOC band calculations resolve the distinct symmetry constraints on the 4H and 6R electronic states. These mechanisms fundamentally differ from conventional approaches by leveraging intrinsic, composition-driven polytypism to modify interlayer coupling and band structure. Thus, by establishing a definitive phase diagram that directly correlates polytypism with superconducting dimensionality, our work provides a clear roadmap for the rational design of low-dimensional superconducting devices through stacking-sequence engineering.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
A Unique Conformationally
Assisted [2+2] Configuration
in Cycloparaphenylenes Enables Efficient Laser Devices
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Two π-conjugated macrocycles, namely the well-known [12]cycloparaphenylene and a newly designed macrocycle combining benzenes and rigid stilbene units, are presented for the first time as light-amplifying gain media in distributed feedback (DFB) laser devices. Both systems show good photonic functionality arising from a four-state photonic cycle comprising a [2+2] state configuration (two delocalized and two conformationally distorted localized states). The mechanism involves the generation of two optically coupled states through excited-state structural distortion induced during internal conversion, which reduces light reabsorption losses and promotes rapid population inversion. Comprehensive steady-state absorption and fluorescence and transient absorption spectroscopy studies are conducted in order to reveal the nature of the low energy lying excited states. Furthermore, amplified spontaneous emission studies of the compounds in polystyrene thin films, followed by the preparation and characterization of optically pumped DFB lasers, were performed. The results reveal new properties of these multifunctional cyclic π-conjugated molecules and unique structure-property relationships.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Enantioconvergent N -Alkylation of Indoles with Alcohols Promoted by an Axially Chiral Iridacycle
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Achieving chemo- and enantioselective N-substitution of indoles presents significant challenges for catalytic method development. Herein, we report an enantioconvergent N-substitution of indoles with racemic secondary alcohols enabled by a newly developed axially chiral biaryl-supported iridacycle and chiral phosphoric acid. This borrowing-hydrogen process proceeds through an intriguing sequence involving transfer hydrogenation of indole, enantioselective reductive amination of an indoline intermediate, and subsequent rearomatization. Controlled reaction temperatures also enable selective access to the N-substituted indolines prior to rearomatization. The catalytic process accommodates diverse indoles and unactivated secondary alcohols without additional stoichiometric reagents, providing a direct and atom-economical approach to enantioenriched N-substituted indoles, including analogs of established drug candidates.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title:
An Allosteric
CLR N-Terminal Swing-Out Mechanism
for RAMP-Mediated Adrenomedullin Receptor Selectivity
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Three receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMP1–3) form heterodimers with the calcitonin (CTR) and calcitonin-like (CLR) G protein-coupled receptors and determine their selectivity for six CGRP family peptide agonists. These ligand–receptor systems are drug targets for migraine headache, diabetes and obesity, and circulatory system disorders. Here, we used molecular dynamics simulations and pharmacological assays of receptor chimeras and point mutants to identify a crucial allosteric component of the mechanism by which RAMP2 and RAMP3 modulate CLR to confer selectivity for two adrenomedullin (AM) peptides. We found that the extracellular domain (ECD) of RAMP2 and RAMP3, but not RAMP1, stabilized a partially unwound “swing-out” conformation of the CLR ECD N-terminal α-helix to accommodate the unique binding mode of the midregion of the AM peptides. The inability of the CTR N-terminus to adopt the swing-out conformation contributed to the distinct peptide selectivity profile of the three CTR-RAMP amylin receptors. By exploiting the CLR swing-out conformation, we engineered AM antagonist peptide variants with enhanced affinity and selectivity for CLR-RAMP2 and -RAMP3. Our results reveal the long-sought mechanism of RAMP-altered CLR ligand selectivity and have significant implications for drug development targeting the CLR- and CTR-RAMP complexes.</jats:p>
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Fast-Charging Sodium Solid-State Batteries Enabled by closo -Hydridoborate Anode Interlayers for Sulfide Electrolytes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sodium solid-state batteries may offer high-power operation through highly conductive sulfide solid electrolytes but remain limited by unstable electrode|electrolyte interfaces. Bilayer separators can decouple interfacial requirements if electrochemical compatibility, contact quality, and charge transfer are ensured. Here, the closo-hydridoborate Na4(B10H10)(B12H12) is identified as an effective interlayer material for sulfide electrolytes. Time-dependent impedance measurements reveal that Na3PS4 bilayer cells still suffer from severe instability, while Na3SbS4 and Na2.9P0.9W0.1S4 bilayers are stabilized by the hydridoborate interlayer. For the latter cells, the interface resistance is easily dominated by poor mechanical contact but can be eliminated under moderate stack pressure. Incorporating Na4(B10H10)(B12H12) enables stable cycling of Na2.9P0.9W0.1S4-based cells with a TiS2-based cathode and Na15Sn4/Na3Sn anode, delivering &gt;90% capacity retention over 250 cycles and capacitor-like charging from 0–50% SOC in 30 s (82 mA cm–2) at 80 °C. The results identify closo-hydridoborate interlayers as key enablers for high-power sodium sulfide solid-state batteries.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Differentiable Solvation Shell Model for Rational Electrolyte Design
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tailoring the Li+ solvation shell is a central design principle for many emerging Li metal battery electrolytes but remains largely qualitative. Here, we introduce a mean-field Ising model that predicts the Li+ solvation shell from the donor number (DN), acceptor number, molar ratio, and molecular size. The model is end-to-end differentiable, enabling direct parameterization from molecular dynamics (MD) solvation structures. For localized high-concentration electrolytes, it reproduces MD shell compositions with 10.7% RMSE at much reduced cost and captures solvation trends in other electrolyte classes without re-fitting. Model interaction terms show that DN dominates Li+ solvation energetics, explaining the empirical DN-based design rules. For LiTFSI in tetraglyme absent from training, the model identifies fluorobenzene as a diluent and a concentration window with anion-rich solvation shells and low free solvent. The predicted solvation structure is confirmed by MD, and published experiments on related electrolytes support the design principles.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Ligand-field reconstruction enables 4.7 V LiCoO 2  with suppressed chemomechanical degradation for high-energy batteries
content: Raising the operating voltage of LiCoO2 cathodes offers a direct and attractive route to higher energy density. However, deep delithiation inevitably triggers severe chemomechanical degradation driven by excessive Co 3d–O 2p orbital hybridization, subsequent lattice oxygen evolution and catastrophic particle fracturing. Here we demonstrate that reconstructing the local transition-metal ligand-field stabilizes the LiCoO2 lattice during ultrahigh-voltage cycling at 4.7 V. By utilizing the moderate ionic potential of fluorine anions to drive this ligand-field reconstruction, we downshift the oxygen 2p band center and thereby decouple detrimental orbital overlap. This targeted electronic regulation dissipates lattice shear stress and minimizes anisotropic lattice distortion. While pristine LiCoO2 accumulates critical stress concentrations reaching 3.0 GPa that initiate extensive intragranular fracturing, our modified architecture alleviates internal stress accumulation and restricts the crack volume ratio to 0.034% after 500 cycles. Consequently, the anion-potential-modified LiCoO2 cathode delivers exceptional durability at 4.7 V, retaining 81.9% capacity over 500 cycles and 71.8% capacity over 1000 cycles at 1C. This work establishes a fundamental design paradigm for high-voltage cathodes, advancing the strategy from conventional surface protection toward intrinsic bulk electronic engineering, and offering a scalable pathway for next-generation high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries.

title: 4 V‐Class Calcium‐Based Water‐in‐Salt Electrolyte for Aqueous Calcium‐Ion Batteries
content:
A 6.2 m Ca(TFSI)2 water‐in‐salt electrolyte delivers a 4.19 V electrochemical stability window and remains liquid at sub‐zero temperatures after adding only 3 wt% acetonitrile. Its ion‐correlated Ca2+‐H2O‐TFSI− solvation structure supports low water activity and fast ion transport. These properties enable aqueous calcium‐ion full cells with stable operation down to −20°C, including a 3.2 V Sn‐based cell.








ABSTRACT
We report the first systematic investigation and demonstration of calcium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (Ca(TFSI)2) as a water‐in‐salt electrolyte for aqueous calcium‐ion batteries (CIBs). At its solubility limit (6.2 m), Ca(TFSI)2 exhibits a surprisingly wide electrochemical stability window (ESW) of 4.19 V, notably with the cathodic limit extending to ‐2.52 V vs Ag/AgCl, significantly surpassing previously reported Ca‐based aqueous electrolytes. Spectroscopic characterization combined with molecular simulations reveals a distinctive solvation structure in which Ca2+ coordinates oxygen atoms from both H2O and TFSI− within the first coordination shell, with an average coordination number of 7. Extensive ion association is also evident through solvent‐shared ion pairs, consistent with suppressed water activity and an expanded ESW. Furthermore, the addition of a small amount of acetonitrile enables the electrolyte to remain liquid at sub‐zero temperatures, while lowering viscosity and enhancing ionic conductivity without substantially disrupting the Ca2+ solvation structure. Leveraging these electrolyte properties, full cells employing perylene‐3,4,9,10‐tetracarboxylic diimide or Sn anodes and a Prussian blue analogue cathode demonstrate robust electrochemical performance at −20°C, including operation over a 3.2 V window with the Sn‐based cell, with long‐term cycling stability and sub‐zero device operation. These findings establish Ca(TFSI)2‐based water‐in‐salt electrolytes as a versatile platform for wide‐voltage, low‐temperature aqueous CIBs.
